questions.questionText: When did the South African War (Second Boer War) begin?
questions.explanation: The war began on 11 October 1899 when Boer forces launched an offensive against British positions.

questions.questionText: What were the two Boer Republics involved in the war?

options.text: South African Republic (Transvaal) and Orange Free State

questions.explanation: The South African Republic (Transvaal) and Orange Free State fought against British forces.

questions.questionText: What were concentration camps used for during the war?

options.text: Detaining Boer civilians and black Africans

questions.explanation: British forces established concentration camps for Boer civilians and black Africans, resulting in high mortality rates.

questions.questionText: Who were the Boers?

options.text: Descendants of Dutch, German, and French settlers

questions.explanation: Boers were descendants of Dutch, German, and French Huguenot settlers who established independent communities.

questions.questionText: What was the outcome of the war for the Boer Republics?

options.text: They lost independence and were annexed by Britain
They became independent in alliance with Britain

questions.explanation: The Treaty of Vereeniging (1902) ended the war with Boer republics surrendering independence to Britain.

questions.questionText: What was Kitchener's strategy to defeat the Boers?

options.text: Scorched earth policy and concentration camps

questions.explanation: Kitchener used scorched earth tactics, destroying farms and moving civilians to camps to break Boer resistance.

questions.questionText: Who led the Boer forces during the war?

options.text: Paul Kruger and other Boer generals

questions.explanation: Paul Kruger, president of the South African Republic, and other generals like De Wet led Boer commandos.

questions.questionText: What were the main causes of the South African War?

options.text: British imperialism, Boer independence, and gold interests

questions.explanation: Causes included British desire to control gold-rich Transvaal, Boer republican independence, and imperial rivalries.

questions.questionText: How were black Africans affected by the war?

options.text: Forced labor, displacement, and detention in concentration camps

questions.explanation: Black Africans faced forced labor, property destruction, and internment in concentration camps regardless of which side they supported.

questions.questionText: What role did guerrilla tactics play in the war?

options.text: Boer commandos used hit-and-run attacks effectively
Guerrilla warfare ended the war quickly

questions.explanation: After losing conventional battles, Boer commandos turned to guerrilla warfare, prolonging the conflict significantly.

questions.questionText: What was the significance of the Treaty of Vereeniging (1902)?

options.text: Ended the war and made Boers British subjects
Divided South Africa into separate states

questions.hint: Peace terms were unfavorable to Boers.
questions.explanation: The treaty required Boer surrender, acceptance of British sovereignty, but promised self-government eventually.

questions.questionText: How did the war affect the relationship between Britain and white South Africans?

options.text: Created lasting resentment but led to eventual reconciliation

questions.explanation: Despite wartime bitterness, post-war policies led to eventual reconciliation culminating in Union and National Party rule.

questions.questionText: What was the role of women in the war?

options.text: Managed farms, supported guerrillas, and suffered in camps

questions.explanation: Boer women managed farms, spied for commandos, and thousands died in concentration camps under harsh conditions.

questions.questionText: Why is the South African War considered a precursor to modern warfare?

options.text: Use of concentration camps, barbed wire, and total war tactics
It was fought with medieval weapons

questions.explanation: The war prefigured WWI with its use of modern weapons, trench warfare, and targeting of civilian populations.

questions.questionText: Evaluate the impact of the concentration camp system on international perceptions of colonialism.

options.text: It exposed colonial brutality and damaged European moral claims

questions.explanation: Reports by Emily Hobhouse exposed conditions in camps, generating international criticism and anti-colonial sentiment.

questions.questionText: Analyze how the war set the stage for racial policies leading to apartheid.

options.text: Victory over black and Boer resistance cemented white supremacy
The war had no connection to apartheid

questions.explanation: Post-war unification of British and Boer white interests, and suppression of black resistance, established foundations for apartheid.

questions.questionText: To what extent did the South African War represent a conflict over economic resources?

options.text: Gold and diamond wealth drove British imperial ambitions

questions.explanation: British capitalists and the uitlander population sought political rights in gold-rich Transvaal, fueling tensions.

questions.questionText: Analyze the legacy of the South African War for modern South African society.

options.text: Created trauma, cemented white dominance, and influenced political developments

questions.explanation: The war's legacy includes physical memorials, cultural trauma, and political trajectories that shaped 20th-century South Africa.

questions.questionText: How did the war influence the path to Union of South Africa in 1910?

options.text: Shared British victory and post-war reconstruction facilitated unity
Union was unrelated to the war

questions.explanation: Post-war cooperation, reconstruction efforts, and the Selborne Memorandum promoting unity among white South Africans led to Union.

questions.questionText: Evaluate the ethical dimensions of Kitchener's scorched earth policy.

options.text: Viewed as necessary but caused widespread suffering and violated customary conduct
Was fully justified under all circumstances

questions.explanation: While considered effective military strategy, the policy caused civilian suffering and anticipated war crimes of later conflicts.
